question.text: A very light, rectangular wire-frame of dimensions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>7</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> hangs just above the free surface of a liquid of surface tension <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math>, with its plane parallel to the free surface. The wire-frame is just brought in contact with the liquid surface and then, lifted up. If the force required to lift the wire-frame is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>36</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></math>, then what is the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>)?

solution.text:
The downward force of surface tension acting on the wire frame is

Fsurface tension=T×l, where l is the total length of the wire which is in contact with the liquid.

Now since it is a wire frame, the free surface of the liquid will be in contact with the inner as well as the outer perimeter of the wire.

Hence, l=2×2×7+5=48 cm

T×48100=3.36 N

⇒T=7 N m-1
